metric.external_integration_coverage.limitations: Sub-scores rely on a small set of declared representative libraries per domain rather than an exhaustive audit of every possible integration; library selection used official project self-designation (official SDK/reference-implementation repos) as the external, benchmark-independent selection rule.
metric.external_integration_coverage.rubric: Frozen rubric applied identically to all 10 languages: score = sum of 5 sub-dimensions x 20 pts, based on the breadth and reliability of officially available or de-facto-standard, actively maintained integration libraries as of the snapshot date. Sub-dimensions: (1) presence and maturity of official first-party SDKs for the three leading cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP); (2) maturity/coverage of relational and NoSQL database client libraries; (3) first-party or reference-implementation support for gRPC/Protocol Buffers RPC/serialization; (4) depth of the container/orchestration ecosystem (Docker/Kubernetes official or reference client libraries); (5) maturity of the messaging/web-framework integration ecosystem (message queues, standard HTTP stack, popular web frameworks).
metric.external_integration_coverage.selection_rule: For each sub-dimension the specific library/target was chosen by a declared external, benchmark-independent criterion: the vendor's own officially designated SDK repository (aws/aws-sdk-go-v2, Azure/azure-sdk-for-go, googleapis/google-cloud-go), the CNCF/Kubernetes project's own reference client (kubernetes/client-go), and the gRPC project's own reference implementation repository (grpc/grpc-go), each retrieved via one route (official project README/package documentation).

cloud_provider_sdks.citation: We are excited to announce the General Availability (GA) release of the AWS SDK for Go version 2 (v2).
cloud_provider_sdks.note: AWS, Azure and GCP each publish and actively maintain official first-party Go SDKs. AWS SDK for Go v2 reached general availability and is described as the official AWS SDK for Go; Google Cloud publishes official Go Cloud Client Libraries; Azure publishes monthly Go SDK releases.

container_orchestration.note: Kubernetes' own official Go client library (client-go) is the reference client for the Kubernetes API, and major container/orchestration infrastructure (Docker, containerd, Kubernetes itself) is implemented in Go, giving the language unusually deep, first-party integration with this domain.

database_drivers.citation: go-redis is the official Redis client library for the Go programming language.
database_drivers.note: Go has a broad, mature database ecosystem: the standard library's database/sql interface plus mature drivers (pgx, go-sql-driver/mysql) for relational databases, an official MongoDB driver, and an official go-redis client for Redis.

messaging_web_ecosystem.citation: NATS Go Client - Go client for the NATS messaging system.
messaging_web_ecosystem.note: Go has a mature messaging ecosystem (official NATS Go client, Confluent's official Kafka Go client, widely used RabbitMQ/AMQP libraries) plus a strong standard-library HTTP stack and popular third-party web frameworks, though some of these (e.g. Kafka, RabbitMQ clients) are community/vendor-maintained rather than uniformly first-party across every messaging system.

rpc_serialization.citation: The Go implementation of gRPC: A high performance, open source, general RPC framework that puts mobile and HTTP/2 first.
rpc_serialization.note: grpc-go is the Go reference implementation of gRPC maintained by the gRPC project itself, alongside official protobuf-go bindings, giving Go first-party, reference-quality RPC/serialization support.

metric.implemented_platform_coverage.limitations: Proxy relies on the vendor-published target-list command/documentation rather than independent verification that every listed target is production-grade; 'go tool dist list' includes some 'known-broken' ports per Go's own porting policy, which the rubric partially penalizes in the other_embedded_legacy_os sub-score.
metric.implemented_platform_coverage.rubric: Frozen rubric applied identically to all 10 languages: score = sum of 5 sub-dimensions x 20 pts, based on breadth of platforms actually supported/shippable by the official toolchain/runtime as of the snapshot date (2026-09-22). Sub-dimensions: (1) tier-1 desktop OS coverage (Windows/macOS/Linux) with first-class official support; (2) breadth of CPU architectures officially supported for native code generation (x86-32/64, ARM 32/64, RISC-V, PPC64, s390x, MIPS, WASM, etc.); (3) mobile OS targets (iOS/Android) reachable via the official toolchain, including whether it is a first-class core capability or requires a secondary/experimental subrepo; (4) Web/WASM target support built into the standard toolchain; (5) breadth of additional/embedded/legacy OS targets (BSD family, Solaris/illumos, AIX, Plan9, z/OS) officially listed and buildable.
metric.implemented_platform_coverage.selection_rule: Source of truth is the Go project's own 'go tool dist list' output and go.dev/doc/install/source GOOS enumeration, cross-checked against secondary reproductions of the same command output. Same retrieval route (official Go docs + reproduced 'go tool dist list' output) used as would be used for any other language's official target-list documentation.

cpu_architecture_breadth.citation: aix/ppc64 android/386 ... linux/riscv64 linux/s390x ... wasip1/wasm windows/386 windows/amd64 windows/arm windows/arm64
cpu_architecture_breadth.note: The official 'go tool dist list' enumerates an unusually broad architecture matrix including 386, amd64, arm, arm64, riscv64, loong64, mips/mips64/mips64le/mipsle, ppc64/ppc64le, s390x, and wasm, spanning nearly every architecture family in current use.

desktop_os_coverage.note: Windows, macOS (darwin) and Linux are all tier-1, first-class, officially supported host and target platforms; Go's own docs demonstrate straightforward cross-compilation to all three from a single machine.

mobile_targets.citation: Choices for $GOOS are android, darwin, dragonfly, freebsd, illumos, ios, js, linux, netbsd, openbsd, plan9, solaris, wasip1, and windows.
mobile_targets.note: android and ios are directly listed as first-party GOOS values in the official install-from-source documentation and in 'go tool dist list' (android/arm64, ios/arm64, etc.), so cross-compiling Go code for phone OSes is a built-in toolchain capability. However, turnkey mobile *application* packaging/UI still depends on the separate golang.org/x/mobile (gomobile) subrepo rather than being a fully first-class, batteries-included app-build pipeline the way it is for some mobile-native languages, so this sub-dimension is scored below the maximum.

other_embedded_legacy_os.citation: FirstClass reports whether goos/goarch is considered a "first class" port.
other_embedded_legacy_os.note: Go officially lists aix, dragonfly, freebsd, illumos, netbsd, openbsd, plan9, solaris and zos (via internal/platform) as buildable GOOS values, which is unusually broad, but the Go porting policy itself classifies some of these ports (e.g. some non-Tier-1 combinations) as non-first-class/'broken' ports subject to lower maintenance guarantees, so this dimension is not scored at the maximum.

web_wasm_targets.note: Go ships official js/wasm and wasip1/wasm GOOS/GOARCH targets directly in the standard toolchain enumeration, giving first-party browser and WASI target support without third-party compilers.
